podcast.body: This hit song, released in 1953, had "Hound Dog" as its B-side. It is one of Elvis Presley's 51 double A-side hits, where both tracks on the single achieved considerable popularity. "Elvis Presley's Houndog was on the other side of Don't Be Cruel back in 1953."

podcast.body: Elvis Presley was fascinated by Billy Ward and the Domino's, particularly their lead singer Jackie Wilson, performing this song in Las Vegas. Elvis believed Wilson's performance was superior to his own, specifically noting Wilson's "Yankee pronunciation" of "Telephone." He later incorporated this same pronunciation into his own performance of the song on the Ed Sullivan Show. "One of the most fascinating elements of the million dollar quartet session is Elvis talking of his experience in Las Vegas, watching Billy Ward and the Domino's singer Elvis's own hit Don't Be Cruel."

podcast.body: In 1956, RCA Records presented Elvis Presley with a gold record for the sale of one million copies of his single "Don't Be Cruel." This was an early, label-specific instance of recognizing a single's immense commercial success before the formalization of industry-wide awards by the RIAA. "In 1956, RCA presented one to Elvis Presley for selling one million copies of his single Don't Be Cruel."

podcast.body: The A-side of Elvis's biggest double-sided hit, definitely chosen by Elvis, and written by Otis Blackwell (credited to Blackwell and Presley due to Colonel Parker's insistence). This song showed a new "lightness of touch" in Elvis's performance, as he was finally in control of the studio sound. It took 28 takes, but resulted in a "light, fluffy sound" where Elvis sounded playful. It was the song that convinced several detractors, including Sam Phillips, of Elvis's ability to make good records away from Sun. It reached number 1 on the charts, then number 2, and along with "Hound Dog," spent 11 weeks at the top. "Elvis's version showed a lightness of touch that had been absent on his earlier RCA records."

podcast.body: This song is mentioned as a benchmark of Elvis Presley's earlier work, used for comparison to his later song "Way Down" in terms of energy and impact. "Does this have the same energy as heartbreak hotel or don't be cruel? Or even suspicious minds? No, it doesn't."
